title: Easy Terminal Proxy Switching on Linux: A Beginner’s Guide
excerpt: A guide for setup alias and bash function for easier proxy ON & OFF
content: Sometimes you want your terminal to send its internet traffic through a VPN or proxy, and sometimes you don’t. Typing long export commands every time gets tedious. This guide shows you how to add three short commands to your terminal: proxy_on turns the proxy on for the current terminal. proxy_off turns it off. proxy_status shows whether it’s on and where it’s pointing. Before You Start You need three things: A running proxy client. This guide uses Clash, which listens on a local “port” (a numbered doorway on your computer) of 7897. Open your Clash app and confirm it’s running. If you use a different client, or a different port, you’ll change the number in the steps below. A terminal. Any terminal app works. Basic comfort with a text editor. You’ll paste a block of text into a file called .bashrc, which is a settings file that runs every time you open a terminal. What’s a proxy? A proxy is a middleman. Your traffic goes to the proxy first, and the proxy forwards it to the internet. This can hide your location or route traffic through a VPN. When the proxy is off, your traffic goes straight out as usual. Step 1: Open Your .bashrc File In your terminal, type: nano ~/.bashrc nano is a simple text editor that runs in the terminal. The ~ symbol means your home folder, so ~/.bashrc is your personal settings file. Scroll to the bottom of the file using the arrow keys. Step 2: Paste the Proxy Functions Copy the block below and paste it at the bottom of the file: # --- Proxy Toggles for Clash Mixed Port --- proxy_on() { export http_proxy="http://127.0.0.1:7897" export https_proxy="http://127.0.0.1:7897" export HTTP_PROXY="http://127.0.0.1:7897" export HTTPS_PROXY="http://127.0.0.1:7897" export all_proxy="socks5h://127.0.0.1:7897" export ALL_PROXY="socks5h://127.0.0.1:7897" alias sudo='sudo -E ' echo -e "\e[1;32m[✔] Terminal proxy routing enabled (127.0.0.1:7897), sudo -E enabled\e[0m" } proxy_off() { unset http_proxy https_proxy HTTP_PROXY HTTPS_PROXY all_proxy ALL_PROXY unalias sudo 2>/dev/null echo -e "\e[1;31m[✘] Terminal proxy routing disabled. sudo -E disabled\e[0m" } proxy_status() { echo "Current Proxy Configuration:" echo "----------------------------" echo "http_proxy = $http_proxy" echo "https_proxy = $https_proxy" echo "all_proxy = $all_proxy" if alias sudo &>/dev/null; then echo "sudo alias = active (sudo -E)" else echo "sudo alias = inactive" fi } Save and exit nano : press Ctrl + O , then Enter to save, then Ctrl + X to exit. Tip: Only paste this block once. If you paste it twice, the functions get defined twice. Nothing breaks, but the file gets messy. Step 3: Load the New Commands Your terminal only reads .bashrc when it starts, so either open a new terminal window or run: source ~/.bashrc Step 4: Try It Out Turn the proxy on: proxy_on You should see a green message confirming the proxy is enabled. Check the status: proxy_status This prints the proxy addresses currently in use and whether the sudo shortcut is active. Turn the proxy off: proxy_off You should see a red message confirming it’s disabled. Step 5: Confirm It Really Works Commands like proxy_on only change your terminal, so the best test is to see whether your internet address changes. Run this while the proxy is on: curl https://ifconfig.me Then run proxy_off and try again. If the address differs between the two runs, the proxy is working. ( curl is a command-line tool for fetching web pages. It’s installed on most Linux systems. On Fedora, you can install it with sudo dnf install curl if needed.) How It Works, in Plain English Each function does a simple job: proxy_on sets several environment variables . These are named notes that programs read when they start. Many command-line tools, such as curl , wget , and git , check these notes and send their traffic through the proxy if they find one. The variables come in both lowercase and uppercase because different programs look for different versions. The socks5h lines use a different proxy protocol called SOCKS5. The h at the end means DNS lookups (converting website names into addresses) also go through the proxy, which avoids leaking which sites you visit. alias sudo='sudo -E ' creates a shortcut so that when you type sudo , it runs as sudo -E . The -E flag keeps your proxy settings when running commands as administrator. Without it, sudo usually wipes your environment, and proxy settings disappear. proxy_off removes all these variables and the sudo shortcut. The 2>/dev/null part hides any error message if the alias was never set. proxy_status prints the current values so you can see what’s active. Troubleshooting command not found: proxy_on You probably didn’t reload your settings. Open a new terminal or run source ~/.bashrc . Also check that you pasted the code into ~/.bashrc and not a different file. The proxy is on, but websites don’t load Your proxy client probably isn’t running, or it’s using a different port. title: A Complete Overhaul For My Personal Tech Blog!
excerpt: Here you are my first post! Announcement for my brand new personal tech blog come online!
content: Hello, everyone, and welcome, fellow netizens! I’m popping in to say hi. My personal website has been sitting on GitHub for about ten years without an update, so it’s time for a renovation. Today I’m launching my brand-new tech blog. It’s simple by design: I write posts in local Markdown files, convert them to HTML, and push them to a remote repository for online display. I did look at plenty of free blog templates on GitHub, but I didn’t need much beyond the basics. As a developer, I mostly use Markdown for code logs and notes, so what I really wanted was a blog that turns Markdown into HTML and serves it online. That’s it. With some help from AI, I built this template in a few hours and spent another hour or two testing it. And ta-da, it’s done! Consider this the official launch day announcement.
